wisniowka: Wiśniówka belongs to the nalewka tradition of Polish country houses, where fruit was steeped in spirit with sugar and the recipes were handed down within families rather than written into any rulebook. Sour cherries, ripe in midsummer, were among the most common choices, and wiśniówka became one of the most familiar of all nalewki. The name comes simply from wiśnia, the Polish word for sour cherry. Commercial distilleries have long bottled their own versions, but home batches, made each summer and opened months later, remain the heart of it.
citron-vodka: Absolut launched Citron in 1988, two years after its pepper-flavoured Peppar, building it on the same Swedish wheat vodka with natural lemon and lime flavour. Toby Cecchini has said that when he reworked the Cosmopolitan at the Odeon in New York, the new Citron was the vodka he reached for, and his version is the one most often credited with spreading the drink, though others claim earlier Cosmopolitans. Rival brands soon followed with citrus vodkas and then many other flavours, and flavoured vodka grew into a crowded category of its own.
swedish-vodka: Swedes have distilled brännvin since at least the fifteenth century, but the clean modern style begins with Lars Olsson Smith, the spirits merchant known as the King of Vodka, who in 1879 launched Absolut Rent Brännvin, 'absolutely pure vodka', made by the then-new method of continuous rectification. A century later the state monopoly Vin & Sprit revived the name for an export vodka distilled at Åhus in Skåne, launched in a clear bottle modelled on an old Swedish apothecary flask. Andy Warhol painted that bottle in 1985, the first of many artists to do so for the brand's advertising.
birch-vodka: Birch sap vodka is a vodka made with the sap that birch trees in the Baltic states and Nordic Europe give for a few weeks each spring, drawing on the region's old custom of tapping and drinking that sap, and no producer or date is credited with the first bottling.
quinoa-vodka: Quinoa vodka is a recent vodka distilled from quinoa, the Andean seed grown for thousands of years around Lake Titicaca in Bolivia and Peru, and its early history as a spirit is not well documented.
feng-aroma-baijiu: Feng-aroma baijiu takes its name from Fengxiang county in western Shaanxi, the home of Xifeng, whose makers claim a local brewing history reaching back thousands of years. Xifeng was named one of China's four famous liquors at the country's first national liquor appraisal, and its method was later recognised as a style of its own, named after the county. It is aged in the jiuhai, a vessel woven from wicker and lined with layers of paper sealed with a paste that traditionally includes pig's blood, lime and beeswax, which is credited with giving the spirit its distinctive flavour.
sesame-aroma-baijiu: Sesame-aroma baijiu was born at the Jingzhi distillery in Anqiu, Shandong, in the 1950s, when the house spirit was found to carry a toasted-sesame note that fitted none of the established styles, although no sesame goes into it. Decades of research into the grains, qu and fermentation behind that note followed before the style was formally recognised as a category of its own, one of the youngest of the major baijiu aroma types. Jingzhi remains its standard-bearer, and distilleries elsewhere in China now make it too.
mixed-aroma-baijiu: Mixed-aroma baijiu, jianxiang, emerged in the twentieth century as distillers began combining the methods of established styles, most often the sauce aroma of Guizhou and the strong aroma of Sichuan, rather than treating them as separate traditions. Its best-known exponent is Baiyunbian of Songzi in Hubei, which takes its name from a line by the Tang poet Li Bai about buying wine on a boat at the edge of the white clouds. Like the other baijiu aroma types, it is defined by a Chinese national standard.
medicinal-aroma-baijiu: Medicinal-aroma baijiu comes from Dongjiu, distilled near the Donggong temple outside Zunyi in Guizhou, which gave the spirit its name. Its method pairs two separate sorghum fermentations, one with a small rice-based qu in small pits and the other with a large wheat-based qu in large pits, the starters made with more than a hundred Chinese herbs between them, and the formula was later classed as a state secret. Dongjiu was named one of China's national famous liquors at the second national appraisal, and its style is now also known as dong aroma, after the house that created it.
soba-shochu: Soba shochu dates from 1973, when Unkai Shuzo released what is credited as the first buckwheat shochu at Gokase, in the mountains of Miyazaki; the brand name, Unkai, means sea of clouds. The lighter style found a following across Japan, and other distilleries took up buckwheat, which despite its name is not a cereal but the seed of a plant related to rhubarb.
kasutori-shochu: Distilling the lees left over from sake brewing is one of the oldest ways of making shochu in Japan, a long-standing practice of the sake breweries of northern Kyushu. Traditionally the lees were packed with rice husks and steamed in wooden steamers, the spent mash went back onto the paddies as fertiliser, and the spirit was linked with sanaburi, the gathering that marked the end of rice planting. After the Second World War the word kasutori was borrowed for rough black-market liquor, a reputation the traditional style has since worked to shake off.
goma-shochu: Goma shochu is the creation of Haruno Hayashida, who established Beniotome Shuzo in 1978 at Tanushimaru, in Kurume, Fukuoka. She had taken charge of the family brewery she married into, which dates from the late seventeenth century, after her husband fell ill, and set out to make a shochu unlike any other by adding roasted sesame to a ferment of barley and rice koji. Beniotome became almost synonymous with the style, and sesame is costly and yields little to ferment, which helps explain why only a handful of distillers have followed.
awamori-kusu: Aged awamori, kusu, comes from the old Ryukyu Kingdom, where distilling is thought to have arrived through trade with Siam around the fifteenth century and the royal court kept awamori to serve visiting envoys. Households and distillers aged it in clay jars and refreshed them by the shitsugi method, pouring a little younger spirit into the oldest jar to replace what was drawn off, so a jar could be kept going for generations. Nearly all the old stock was lost in the Battle of Okinawa at the end of the Second World War, and today's kusu is a rebuilt tradition.
sato: Sato is the village rice drink of Isan, Thailand's north-east, brewed from sticky rice with luk paeng, a dried starter cake of rice flour, herbs and wild yeasts and moulds; the same ferment distilled becomes the stronger lao khao. Families made it for festivals, merit-making and the rice harvest. Thai law long restricted brewing and distilling at home, and in the early twenty-first century the rules were eased so that licensed community producers could make and sell it, which helped bring bottled sato from the villages to wider markets.
ruou-nep: In northern Vietnam rượu nếp names two things made from the same grain: the sweet fermented sticky rice eaten as a dish, and the clear spirit distilled from it. The prized grain is nếp cái hoa vàng, a fragrant glutinous rice of the Red River delta, and villages such as Vân in Bắc Giang built reputations on their distilling over generations. The fermented rice itself is eaten at Tết Đoan Ngọ, the festival on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, traditionally first thing in the morning. No single maker is credited with the spirit; it is a village tradition.
colombian-aguardiente: Cane spirit has been distilled in Colombia since colonial times, when the Spanish crown controlled aguardiente as a royal monopoly to raise revenue. Early in the twentieth century the right to run that monopoly passed to the departments, and in 1920 Antioquia opened the Fábrica de Licores de Antioquia in Medellín to produce its own. Its anise-flavoured Aguardiente Antioqueño became the department's emblem and travelled well beyond it, while other departments bottle their own rivals, such as the Valle del Cauca's Blanco del Valle, and loyalty to the local brand runs deep.
absinthe-verte: The usual story credits Pierre Ordinaire, a French doctor living in the Swiss Val-de-Travers, with an absinthe elixir in the 1790s, though the Henriod sisters of Couvet are more securely documented making it. Their recipe passed to Major Daniel-Henri Dubied, who in 1798 opened a distillery in Couvet with his son-in-law Henri-Louis Pernod. In 1805 Pernod moved across the border to Pontarlier, and the green, naturally coloured absinthe of France became the drink of Belle Époque cafés until bans in Switzerland in 1910 and France in 1915.
absinthe-blanche: Absinthe was born in the Val-de-Travers in the late eighteenth century, but the clear style as it is known today is a child of its ban. When Switzerland outlawed absinthe in 1910, the valley's distillers carried on in secret, dropping the colouring step and bottling the spirit straight off the still, since a colourless bottle was easier to explain to an inspector than a vivid green one. Locally it became known as la bleue. Switzerland legalised absinthe again in 2005, and Val-de-Travers producers now make blanche openly, the style having outlived the reason for it.
dill-aquavit: Aquavit enters the written record in the sixteenth century, when Eske Bille, the Danish lord of Bergenhus castle in Norway, sent 'some water which is called Aqua Vite' to the Archbishop of Norway. Caraway became the defining flavour across Scandinavia, but Danish and Swedish distillers also made versions led by dill, the herb that seasons so much of the Nordic summer table, from crayfish to new potatoes. When the European Union defined the category, it named caraway and dill as the only permitted lead flavours, which makes dill aquavit one of the two pillars of the style.
taffel-akvavit: Taffel akvavit is bound up with Aalborg, in northern Jutland, where Isidor Henius, a distiller from Toruń, made his name with a clean, caraway-led spirit; the brand gives 1846 as its starting date. His Aalborg Taffel Akvavit, nicknamed Rød Aalborg for its red label, became Denmark's best-known akvavit, and in 1881 his business was merged into De Danske Spritfabrikker. Taffel means table, and the name marks it as the everyday bottle for the lunch table rather than an aged or special one.
kruidenbitter: Dutch kruidenbitters grew from the old habit of steeping herbs and roots in jenever, and the most famous takes its name from Hendrik Beerenburg, an Amsterdam spice merchant on the Stromarkt who sold a herb mixture for customers to steep in their own spirit. The drink found its real following in the northern provinces, above all Friesland, where distillers such as Sonnema later bottled it ready-made. Many other towns and families kept their own kruidenbitter recipes.
tuica-de-prune-batrana: Horincă is the Maramureș name for the fruit brandy distilled across Romania, and the word reflects the region's place on the Ukrainian border: it is related to the Ukrainian horilka, from a Slavic root meaning to burn. Families distil plums or apples in small copper stills, often twice, and the spirit is poured for guests and at weddings and funerals. The same tradition goes by other names elsewhere, țuică in the south and pălincă in Transylvania. No single maker is credited with horincă; it belongs to the villages of the north.
rakia-medena: Medovina rakija is a rare Balkan spirit distilled from fermented honey, the base of mead, rather than rakija sweetened with honey afterwards like medovača, and no producer, village or date is credited with it as a style.
macallan12sherryoak-sb: The Macallan was founded in 1824 by Alexander Reid, a farmer who took out one of the first licences under the new Excise Act on the Easter Elchies estate, above a ford on the Spey near Craigellachie used by cattle drovers. Its reputation came to rest on sherry casks, which the distillery has made to order in Spain and seasoned with oloroso in Jerez before filling. The 12-year-old took the name Sherry Oak when Macallan added a Fine Oak range alongside it, and in 2018 the house moved into a new distillery built into the hillside.
macallan18sherryoak-sb: Macallan's story begins in 1824 with Alexander Reid's licence on the Easter Elchies estate in Speyside, and its long-aged sherry whiskies did much to make its name among collectors. For many years the 18-year-old's label carried the year it was distilled, so each annual release could be told apart. It is matured only in oak casks seasoned with oloroso sherry in Jerez, and Easter Elchies House, the early-eighteenth-century manor on the estate, still appears on the label.
glenfiddich12-sb: William Grant worked for twenty years at Mortlach before building his own distillery in Dufftown, with the help of his children and a single stonemason, using second-hand stills bought from Cardhu. The first spirit ran on Christmas Day 1887. He called it Glenfiddich, Gaelic for valley of the deer, which is why a stag appears on the label. The family firm, still independent, was among the first to promote single malt abroad in the 1960s, when almost all malt whisky disappeared into blends, and the 12-year-old is its signature bottling today.
glenfiddich15solera-sb: Glenfiddich has been distilled in Dufftown since 1887, when William Grant's family filled their first casks on Christmas Day. The 15-year-old Solera was created in 1998 by the malt master David Stewart, who borrowed the solera idea from the sherry bodegas of Jerez: whisky aged in bourbon, sherry and new oak casks is married in a large vat of Oregon pine that is never emptied below half, so every batch carries a little of the ones before it. The vat has been topped up continuously since it was first filled.
glenfiddich18-sb: Glenfiddich began in 1887 in Dufftown, where William Grant and his family built the distillery stone by stone, and it is still owned by his descendants. The house keeps its own coopers and coppersmiths on site, unusual for a distillery of its size, and has long been bottled in a distinctive triangular bottle. The 18-year-old, once sold as Ancient Reserve, is aged in a mix of oloroso sherry and bourbon casks and married in small batches before bottling, a deeper, longer-aged expression of the same Speyside spirit.
glenlivet12-sb: George Smith had distilled illicitly on his farm at Upper Drummin for years before taking out one of the first licences under the new Excise Act in 1824, with the backing of his landlord the Duke of Gordon, and he is said to have carried a pair of pistols for protection from smugglers who saw him as a traitor. After a fire, production moved to Minmore in 1859. So many distillers borrowed the valley's name that Smith's son went to court, and from then on only his whisky could be called The Glenlivet, while others had to add their own names.
glenlivet18-sb: The Glenlivet traces its licence to 1824, when George Smith became one of the first legal distillers in a remote glen famous for smuggling, where illicit whisky had long been carried over the hills to the Lowlands. The name became such a mark of quality that many Speyside rivals tacked it onto their own, earning Glenlivet the joking title of the longest glen in Scotland. The 18-year-old, matured in a mix of American and European oak, is a longer-aged expression of the same house spirit.
glenlivetnadurra-sb: George Smith's licence of 1824 made Glenlivet one of the first legal distilleries in Speyside, in a glen where illicit stills had been the rule. Nàdurra, Gaelic for natural, was introduced in the mid-2000s as the distillery's take on whisky bottled the old way: at cask strength, without chill filtration, and in its first batches from first-fill bourbon casks. Each batch carries its own strength and batch code, and later releases have varied the wood, including oloroso sherry casks and casks that once held peated whisky.
balveniedoublewood12-sb: William Grant founded Balvenie in 1892, next to his Glenfiddich distillery in Dufftown, by converting an eighteenth-century mansion, and named it after the ruined Balvenie Castle nearby. It still keeps its own malting floor, coppersmith and coopers. DoubleWood is the work of malt master David Stewart, whose experiments with moving whisky from one cask to another helped popularise cask finishing across the industry: it spends most of its life in American oak before a final period in European oak casks that held sherry.
balveniecaribbeancask14-sb: Balvenie was founded in 1892 by William Grant, whose family still owns it alongside Glenfiddich next door, and it is one of the few Scotch distilleries to grow some of its own barley and turn it on a traditional malting floor. Caribbean Cask is another of malt master David Stewart's cask experiments: it spends fourteen years in American oak before being finished in casks that the distillery seasons itself with a blend of West Indian rums, a twist on the cask finishing Stewart had pioneered at Balvenie.
balvenieportwood21-sb: Balvenie dates from 1892, when William Grant began converting a mansion beside his Glenfiddich distillery in Dufftown, and it first distilled the following spring. PortWood 21 came out of David Stewart's long run of cask experiments there: it is drawn from whiskies aged at least twenty-one years in oak and then finished in port pipes, the large casks used for port. Stewart, who joined the company as an apprentice in 1962, became one of the longest-serving malt masters in Scotch whisky.
aberlour12-sb: James Fleming founded Aberlour in 1879 in the Speyside village of the same name, near a spring traditionally linked to St Drostan, a sixth-century missionary. After a fire in 1898 the distillery was rebuilt to a design by Charles Doig, the architect behind many Victorian distilleries. Pernod Ricard, the present owner, has made the house known for maturing its whisky in both sherry and bourbon casks, and the 12-year-old is a marriage of the two.
aberlourabunadh-sb: Aberlour has been distilling where the Lour burn meets the Spey since 1879. A'bunadh, Gaelic for of the origin, was introduced in the late 1990s, and the house story is that it was inspired by an old bottle found during building work at the distillery, wrapped in a newspaper from the 1890s. It is matured in oloroso sherry butts, bottled at cask strength without chill filtration and released in numbered batches, each with its own strength.
glenfarclas15-sb: Robert Hay licensed Glenfarclas in 1836 at Rechlerich farm, at the foot of Ben Rinnes in Speyside, and in 1865 it was bought by John Grant and his son George, whose descendants still run it. The name is usually translated as valley of the green grassland. The family has kept direct-fired stills and a strong preference for sherry casks, and as one of the few Scotch distilleries still in family hands it has stayed out of the large drinks groups. The 15-year-old is matured largely in oloroso sherry butts.
glenfarclas105-sb: Glenfarclas, licensed in 1836 near Ben Rinnes, has been run by the Grant family since 1865. In 1968 the family introduced the 105, named for its strength of 105 degrees on the old British proof scale, about 60 per cent alcohol, and it was one of the first single malts sold at cask strength. Like most Glenfarclas, it draws heavily on sherry casks.
glendronach12-sb: James Allardice founded GlenDronach in 1826 in the Valley of Forgue in Aberdeenshire, naming it after the Dronac burn that runs past it, and he was among the first distillers licensed under the new excise rules. The house is best known for whisky matured in Spanish sherry casks, and the 12-year-old, first released as Original, combines Pedro Ximénez and oloroso. The distillery was silent from 1996 to 2002, Billy Walker's BenRiach company bought it in 2008, and Brown-Forman acquired it in 2016.
glendronach18allardice-sb: GlenDronach was founded in 1826 by James Allardice, and the 18-year-old carries his name. The distillery tells a story that Allardice, failing to interest Edinburgh's gentlemen in his whisky, gave some to women of the Cowgate, whose recommendation is said to have made it fashionable. The Allardice is matured entirely in oloroso sherry casks, and the distillery near Forgue was among the last in Scotland to fire its stills directly with coal, a practice that ended in 2005.
cragganmore12-sb: John Smith, a distiller who had managed Macallan, Glenlivet and Glenfarclas, founded Cragganmore in 1869 at Ballindalloch, choosing the site for its spring water and for the new Strathspey railway beside it. It was one of the first distilleries built to use rail, with its own siding to carry casks away. Its unusual flat-topped spirit stills help give the whisky its complex character, and in 1988 the 12-year-old was chosen to represent Speyside in the Classic Malts range.
mortlach16-sb: Mortlach was the first legal distillery in Dufftown, founded in 1823 by James Findlater, and the town grew into one of the capitals of Speyside whisky around it. William Grant worked there for twenty years before leaving to build Glenfiddich. Its stills run a complex, partial triple distillation that the distillery describes as 2.81 times, giving a heavy, meaty spirit nicknamed the Beast of Dufftown. For decades it went mostly into blends, until Diageo relaunched it as a single malt; the 16-year-old Distiller's Dram arrived in 2018.
benriachthetwelve-sb: John Duff built BenRiach in 1897 beside his Longmorn distillery near Elgin, but the collapse of the blenders Pattisons left it silent from 1900 until 1965, while its malting floors kept supplying Longmorn. Under later owners it became known for unusual cask work, and in 2004 a group led by Billy Walker bought it. The Twelve, a marriage of bourbon, sherry and port casks, was introduced by master blender Rachel Barrie after Brown-Forman acquired the distillery in 2016.
glengrant12-sb: Brothers James and John Grant founded Glen Grant in Rothes in 1840. James's son, also James and known as the Major, gave it tall, slender stills fitted with purifiers, which still shape its light, fruity spirit, and he was among the first in the Highlands to have electric light. He also laid out the Victorian woodland garden behind the distillery. In the decades after the Second World War Glen Grant became a favourite in Italy, and Campari has owned it since 2006.
longmorn16-sb: Longmorn was built in 1893 near Elgin by John Duff, Charles Shirres and George Thomson, and began distilling at the end of the following year; Duff went on to build BenRiach next door. Prized by blenders, Longmorn has spent most of its life as a component of blends, today under Chivas Brothers, and official single malt bottlings have been comparatively rare. The 16-year-old was for some years the distillery's main release. The name is often said to recall an old chapel site, though its exact meaning is uncertain.
craigellachie13-sb: Craigellachie was built in 1891 in the village where the Fiddich meets the Spey, by a partnership that included Peter Mackie of White Horse, to a design by Charles Doig. It still condenses its spirit in old-fashioned worm tubs, which give the whisky a heavy, sulphury edge that blenders valued. John Dewar and Sons, part of Bacardi, bought it in 1998, and the 13-year-old was part of the range that brought Craigellachie out as a single malt in its own right in 2014.
speyburn10-sb: Speyburn was built in 1897 by John Hopkins and Company in a narrow glen near Rothes, to a design by Charles Doig. Its owners were determined to fill a cask in Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee year, so distilling began on 15 December in a snowstorm, before the doors and windows had been fitted, and one butt was filled bearing that year's date. Speyburn was also an early user of pneumatic drum maltings. Inver House Distillers has owned it since the early 1990s.
tamdhu12-sb: Tamdhu, Gaelic for little dark hill, was established in 1896 by a group of whisky blenders in the Speyside parish of Knockando, and its first spirit was casked in 1897. It was mothballed several times, most recently in 2010, before Ian Macleod Distillers bought it in 2011 and restarted production in 2013. The new owners relaunched Tamdhu as a whisky matured entirely in sherry casks. For decades it had also been one of the last distilleries to malt its own barley mechanically, in Saladin boxes.
glenrothes12-sb: Glenrothes filled its first casks on 28 December 1879, the same night as the Tay Bridge disaster, in the Speyside town of Rothes. It soon became part of what grew into Highland Distillers, and for most of its life it supplied blends such as Cutty Sark and The Famous Grouse. The wine merchants Berry Bros and Rudd owned the brand for some years, and in 2018 Edrington relaunched the single malt with age statements in its Soleo Collection, of which the 12-year-old is a core bottling.
strathisla12-sb: Strathisla was founded in 1786 as the Milltown distillery in Keith, on the River Isla, and is often described as the oldest working distillery in the Highlands. Its twin pagoda roofs and cobbled courtyard keep the look of an old farm distillery. Seagram's Chivas Brothers bought it at auction in 1950, making it the spiritual home of Chivas Regal, and adopted the name Strathisla, the broad valley of the Isla, for the distillery as well as its whisky.
knockando12-sb: John Tytler Thomson built Knockando in 1898 above the Spey, and in 1904 it was bought by W and A Gilbey, the London gin producers, whose business was later merged with Justerini and Brooks; its whisky has long been part of the heart of J&B. The name is usually translated as hill of commerce, from the Gaelic Cnoc Cheannachd. Knockando is known for bottling by vintage, with the distillation and bottling years on the label, so the 12-year-old is really a vintage of around twelve years.
linkwood12-sb: Peter Brown, factor to the Seafield estates, founded Linkwood near Elgin in 1821, and his son William rebuilt it in the 1870s. Its light, floral spirit has gone mostly into blends, and the distillery is remembered for a mid-twentieth-century manager, Roderick Mackenzie, who is said to have refused to let anything be changed, down to the cobwebs, in case it altered the whisky. The 12-year-old was released in the Flora and Fauna series, which brought many little-known malts to bottle.
benriachsmokyten-sb: BenRiach was built in 1897 by John Duff beside Longmorn and, after a long silence, reopened in 1965. In the following decades it began distilling a peated spirit alongside its usual unpeated one, unusual for Speyside and originally intended for blending. Under later owners peated BenRiach became a feature of the range, and Smoky Ten, matured in bourbon barrels, Jamaican rum casks and toasted virgin oak, was introduced when master blender Rachel Barrie reworked the core range.
ardbeg10-sb: Ardbeg's commercial history starts in 1815, when John MacDougall founded a distillery on the south coast of Islay, though distilling on the site may be older. It made some of the most heavily peated whisky on the island, but it fell silent in 1981 and ran only intermittently until Glenmorangie bought it in 1997 and restored it. The Ten became the flagship of the revival, bottled at 46 per cent without chill filtration, and helped build a devoted following for intensely peated malts.
ardbeguigeadail-sb: Ardbeg was founded in 1815 on Islay's south coast and revived by Glenmorangie in the late 1990s. Uigeadail takes its name from Loch Uigeadail, the hill loch above the distillery that supplies its peaty water. Released in the early 2000s, it marries young peated Ardbeg from bourbon casks with older whisky matured in sherry butts, and is bottled at cask strength without an age statement. It became one of the cornerstones of Ardbeg's core range alongside the Ten.
ardbegcorryvreckan-sb: Ardbeg, founded in 1815 on the south coast of Islay, has named several releases after local landmarks. Corryvreckan takes its name from the whirlpool in the strait between Jura and Scarba, north of Islay, one of the largest in the world and famous in Hebridean lore. It began as a release for members of the Ardbeg Committee, the distillery's enthusiasts' club, before joining the core range in place of Airigh Nam Beist, and it adds French oak casks to the usual bourbon barrels.
lagavulin16-sb: Lagavulin was founded in 1816 by John Johnston on the south coast of Islay, although illicit stills are said to have worked the bay long before. The name comes from the Gaelic for hollow where the mill is. In the early twentieth century Peter Mackie, whose family firm owned it and used it in White Horse, built a second distillery on the site, Malt Mill, to try to reproduce the whisky of his neighbour Laphroaig after losing its agency. The 16-year-old became Lagavulin's signature when it joined the Classic Malts range in 1988.
lagavulin8-sb: Lagavulin has distilled on Islay's south shore since 1816. When the Victorian writer Alfred Barnard toured the distilleries of Britain in the 1880s, he tasted an eight-year-old Lagavulin and praised it highly, and in 2016 the distillery marked its two-hundredth anniversary with a new eight-year-old in his honour. Younger and brighter than the long-established 16-year-old, it was meant as a limited release but went on to join the permanent range.
laphroaig10-sb: Brothers Alexander and Donald Johnston founded Laphroaig in 1815 on the south coast of Islay, and the name is usually translated as the beautiful hollow by the broad bay. In 1954 Bessie Williamson, who had arrived as a temporary secretary two decades earlier, inherited the distillery and ran it, one of very few women to lead a Scotch distillery in the twentieth century. The story goes that its pungent, iodine-like aroma helped it into America during Prohibition as a medicine. The 10-year-old is its long-standing flagship.
laphroaigquartercask-sb: Laphroaig has been distilled on Islay since 1815, when the Johnston brothers set up on the south coast. Quarter Cask revives a nineteenth-century practice: small casks, about a quarter the size of a sherry butt, were easier to carry by packhorse and gave whisky more contact with the wood. Laphroaig introduced it in the mid-2000s, finishing whisky first aged in bourbon barrels in these small casks, and it soon became a permanent part of the range.
laphroaiglore-sb: Laphroaig dates from 1815, and its methods, from its own floor maltings to peat cut on Islay and the smoky kiln that dries the barley, have been handed down through generations of distillery workers. Lore was introduced in 2016 as a tribute to that handed-down knowledge, blending whiskies of different ages drawn from several cask types. Its name, the house says, refers to the lore passed from one generation of Laphroaig distillers to the next.
bowmore12-sb: Bowmore is the oldest distillery on Islay, founded in 1779 by John Simson, a local merchant, on the shore of Loch Indaal in the village of the same name. Its No. 1 Vaults, partly below sea level, are said to be among the oldest whisky warehouses in Scotland. The distillery still turns part of its own barley on traditional malting floors and dries it over Islay peat, and its whisky sits between the heavily peated malts of the south coast and the gentler ones of the north. Suntory has owned it since the 1990s.
bowmore15darkest-sb: Bowmore, founded in 1779 by John Simson on the shore of Loch Indaal, is Islay's oldest licensed distillery. The 15-year-old, long sold as Darkest, is matured in bourbon casks before spending its final years in oloroso sherry casks, which give it the deep colour behind its name. Bowmore's warehouses sit right on the sea wall, and the distillery is one of the few in Scotland still malting some of its own barley by hand on traditional floors.
bruichladdichclassicladdie-sb: Bruichladdich was built in 1881 by the Harvey brothers, a Glasgow distilling family, on the shore of Loch Indaal on Islay's Rhinns. After years of changing owners it closed in 1994, until a group led by Mark Reynier and Simon Coughlin bought it in 2000, brought in the veteran distiller Jim McEwan and reopened it the following year with its Victorian equipment. The Classic Laddie, unpeated and made from Scottish barley, became the flagship of the revived house, a deliberate contrast to Islay's smoky malts. Rémy Cointreau bought the distillery in 2012.
portcharlotte10-sb: Port Charlotte is the heavily peated whisky Bruichladdich began distilling in 2001, the year the distillery reopened. It is named after the village a couple of miles south along Loch Indaal, which was home to the Lochindaal distillery until it closed in 1929. The first bottlings appeared from the mid-2000s, and the 10-year-old became the range's flagship, made from Scottish barley peated to around 40 parts per million and matured on Islay.
octomore-sb: Octomore takes its name from a farm above Port Charlotte on Islay, where a small distillery worked in the early nineteenth century. Bruichladdich revived the name for an experiment in extreme peating, first distilled in 2002 and released in 2008, using barley dried over peat smoke for far longer than usual; that first edition measured 131 parts per million of phenols. Each edition since has been numbered and released in small runs, mostly built on young whisky to keep the smoke at the fore.
caolila12-sb: Hector Henderson founded Caol Ila in 1846 near Port Askaig, facing the Paps of Jura across the narrow Sound of Islay, which gives the distillery its Gaelic name. It was rebuilt almost entirely in the 1970s and is now the largest distillery on Islay, much of its peated spirit going into blends such as Johnnie Walker. Diageo began releasing it regularly as a single malt in the early 2000s, with the 12-year-old as its core bottling.
bunnahabhain12-sb: Bunnahabhain was built in 1881 by a company of Glasgow blenders at a remote bay on the north-east coast of Islay, with a pier, cottages and a road built along with it. The name is Gaelic for mouth of the river, after the Margadale river that meets the sea there. Unlike most Islay malts it has been made mainly from unpeated barley, and its gentler spirit went largely into blends such as Cutty Sark and The Famous Grouse. The 12-year-old is bottled at 46.3 per cent without chill filtration.
kilchomanmachirbay-sb: Anthony Wills founded Kilchoman in 2005 as a farm distillery on the west of Islay, the first new distillery on the island in about a century, and it is one of the few in Scotland to grow, malt, distil, mature and bottle on site. Machir Bay, its core release, is named after the long beach a short walk from the distillery, and is made from peated barley matured mostly in bourbon barrels with a finish in oloroso sherry casks. The family-owned distillery bought Rockside Farm, where it had always grown barley, in 2015.
ardnahoe-sb: Ardnahoe opened in 2019 on the north-east coast of Islay, between Caol Ila and Bunnahabhain, overlooking the Sound of Islay towards Jura. It was built by Hunter Laing, the family firm of independent bottlers led by Stewart Laing and his sons, and its name is Gaelic for height of the hollow, shared with the loch beside it. Unusually for Islay it condenses its spirit in worm tubs, and its first single malt, a five-year-old from bourbon and oloroso casks, was released in 2024.
talisker10-sb: Hugh and Kenneth MacAskill founded Talisker in 1830 at Carbost, on the shore of Loch Harport on the Isle of Skye, naming it after Talisker House nearby, and for most of its history it was the only distillery on the island. Robert Louis Stevenson named it among the king of drinks in an 1880 poem, alongside Islay and Glenlivet. Its peppery, maritime character made the 10-year-old the island representative when the Classic Malts range was launched in 1988.
taliskerstorm-sb: Talisker has distilled on the Isle of Skye since 1830, when the MacAskill brothers built it at Carbost on Loch Harport. Storm was introduced in 2013 as a no-age-statement bottling with a smokier, more intense character than the long-established 10-year-old, made from a vatting that includes rejuvenated casks. Its name nods to the Atlantic weather that batters the island's west coast, where the distillery sits a short walk from the sea loch.
highlandpark12-sb: Highland Park gives 1798 as its founding year, and Orkney tradition credits the site to Magnus Eunson, a smuggler and church officer said to have hidden whisky under the pulpit. The distillery stands on the edge of Kirkwall and still turns some of its own barley on malting floors, drying it over peat from Hobbister Moor, rich in heather because Orkney has so few trees. The 12-year-old, renamed Viking Honour in 2017, nods to the islands' Norse heritage.
highlandpark18-sb: Highland Park, in Kirkwall on Orkney, traces its founding to 1798 and is one of the most northerly whisky distilleries in Scotland. It matures much of its whisky in sherry-seasoned oak, a long-standing house practice, and the aromatic heather peat cut on Orkney's Hobbister Moor gives the spirit its characteristic smoke. The 18-year-old, now called Viking Pride, has long been one of the distillery's most celebrated bottlings and did much to build its reputation among whisky writers.
scapaskiren-sb: Scapa was founded in 1885 by Macfarlane and Townsend on the shore of Scapa Flow, the great natural harbour south of Kirkwall that served as a Royal Navy base in both world wars. It is known for its Lomond-type wash still, a rare design with a thick, straight neck, and its whisky is unpeated, unlike its Orkney neighbour Highland Park. Skiren, Old Norse for glittering bright skies, was introduced in 2015 when Pernod Ricard relaunched the single malt and opened the distillery to visitors.
jura10-sb: A distillery was licensed at Craighouse on the Isle of Jura in 1810, but it fell into ruin early in the twentieth century. In the early 1960s two local landowners, Robin Fletcher and Tony Riley-Smith, rebuilt it to bring work back to an island of only a few hundred people, with tall stills designed to make a lighter, Highland-style spirit. Jura remains one of the most remote distilleries in Scotland, and its single malt, of which the 10-year-old is the entry point, takes its identity from the island.
arran10-sb: The Isle of Arran distillery opened at Lochranza in 1995, the first legal distillery on the island in well over a century, founded by Harold Currie, a former director at Chivas and a D-Day veteran. Construction was briefly halted when a pair of protected golden eagles nested on the cliffs nearby. The 10-year-old, among the first age-stated bottlings from the young distillery, became the core of its range, and a second distillery at Lagg, in the south of the island, followed in 2019 to make peated spirit.
tobermory12-sb: Tobermory, in the harbour town of the same name on the Isle of Mull, was founded in 1798 by John Sinclair, a local merchant, and is one of the oldest commercial distilleries in Scotland. It has been silent for long stretches, including much of the twentieth century, and has changed hands many times. It makes two spirits, unpeated Tobermory and peated Ledaig. After a refurbishment in the late 2010s the unpeated range was relaunched with the 12-year-old at its core.
ledaig10-sb: Ledaig was the original name of the distillery John Sinclair founded in 1798 at Tobermory on the Isle of Mull, and comes from the Gaelic for safe haven. Today the name belongs to the distillery's peated spirit, made from heavily peated barley alongside the unpeated Tobermory, which gives Mull a smoky malt to set beside Islay's. Ledaig has grown into a range of its own, and the 10-year-old is its core release.
glenmorangieoriginal10-sb: William Matheson licensed Glenmorangie in 1843 at Tain, on the Dornoch Firth, converting a farm brewery at Morangie. He is said to have equipped it with second-hand gin stills, and their descendants are still the tallest in Scotland, with necks over five metres high, which help give the spirit its light, fruity character. The house translates its name as glen of tranquillity. The 10-year-old, matured in American oak, was renamed The Original in the 2000s, and LVMH has owned the distillery since 2004.
glenmorangielasanta-sb: Glenmorangie, licensed at Tain in 1843, made its name with an unusually light spirit from Scotland's tallest stills. Under Bill Lumsden, its director of whisky creation, the house became a pioneer of extra maturation, moving whisky from bourbon casks into casks that had held wines. Lasanta, from a Gaelic phrase the distillery translates as warmth and passion, spends its extra time in oloroso and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, and it replaced the earlier Sherry Wood Finish when the range was relaunched in 2007.
glenmorangiequintaruban-sb: Glenmorangie has distilled at Tain on the Dornoch Firth since 1843, and since the 1990s it has been known for finishing whisky in wine casks. Quinta Ruban, which replaced the old Port Wood Finish in 2007, takes its name from the Portuguese word for a wine estate and the Gaelic for ruby, after the colour it gains from its time in ruby port casks from the Douro. The current version is aged fourteen years, the last four of them in port casks.
glenmorangiesignet-sb: Glenmorangie was licensed in 1843 at Tain, and its tall stills have long given it a light, delicate spirit. Signet, introduced in 2008, was Bill Lumsden's attempt at something much richer: it includes a portion of whisky made with chocolate malt, barley roasted at high temperature as brewers do for stouts, blended with some of the distillery's oldest stocks and whisky matured in new oak casks. Like every Glenmorangie, it carries an emblem taken from the Hilton of Cadboll stone, a Pictish slab found near Tain.
dalmore12-sb: Alexander Matheson founded Dalmore in 1839 on the Cromarty Firth at Alness, and from 1867 it was run by the Mackenzie family. The stag on every bottle comes from the Mackenzie arms and a clan legend that an ancestor saved a Scottish king from a charging stag in the thirteenth century, after which the family was granted the right to bear a stag's head. Whyte and Mackay owns the distillery today, and Richard Paterson, its master blender for decades, is closely associated with the sherry-led house style.
dalmore15-sb: Dalmore has distilled on the Cromarty Firth since 1839, founded by Alexander Matheson and run for generations by the Mackenzie family, whose royal stag still decorates its bottles. The distillery's stills are unusual, some with water jackets cooling their necks, and its house style leans on sherry. The 15-year-old is matured in American white oak before being finished in three kinds of sherry casks, Matusalem, Apóstoles and Amoroso, then married together before bottling.
oban14-sb: Brothers John and Hugh Stevenson founded Oban distillery in 1794, before the town had grown up around it, and it now sits squeezed between the main street and the cliff beneath McCaig's Tower, with no room to expand. With just two stills it is one of the smallest distilleries owned by Diageo. Its whisky sits between the soft Highland malts and the peated island ones, and the 14-year-old was chosen to represent the West Highlands when the Classic Malts range was launched in 1988.
dalwhinnie15-sb: Dalwhinnie was built in 1897 as the Strathspey distillery near the Drumochter Pass, at about 350 metres one of the highest distilleries in Scotland, where old drovers' roads met; the name comes from the Gaelic for meeting place. In 1905 it became the first Scotch distillery owned by an American company, Cook and Bernheimer. Its cold climate and worm tub condensers shape its honeyed spirit, and the 15-year-old represented the Highlands in the Classic Malts range from 1988.
glenmorangie18-sb: Glenmorangie has been made at Tain since 1843, and the distillery's emblem comes from the Hilton of Cadboll stone, a Pictish cross-slab carved around the eighth century, found nearby and now in the National Museum of Scotland. The 18-year-old, once labelled Extremely Rare, spends fifteen years in bourbon casks before part of the whisky is moved into oloroso sherry casks for its final years and married back with the rest.
oldpulteney12-sb: James Henderson founded Pulteney in 1826 in Wick, Caithness, in Pulteneytown, a planned fishing settlement laid out by the British Fisheries Society and named after its governor Sir William Pulteney. The distillery grew up with the herring trade, when barley and supplies arrived by sea, and its whisky came to be called the maritime malt. It fell silent in 1930, while Wick had voted itself dry, and reopened in 1951. Inver House owns it today.
clynelish14-sb: The first Clynelish distillery was founded in 1819 at Brora, in Sutherland, by the Marquess of Stafford, later Duke of Sutherland, partly to give a market for barley grown by tenants moved to the coast during the Highland Clearances. A new distillery was built beside it in the late 1960s and took the Clynelish name, while the old one, renamed Brora, closed in 1983 and was revived in 2021. Clynelish's famously waxy spirit is a key part of Johnnie Walker blends, and the 14-year-old is its main single malt.
glenallachie12-sb: GlenAllachie was built in 1967 near Aberlour in Speyside, designed by William Delmé-Evans for Mackinlay McPherson, and for half a century it worked almost unseen, supplying blends. In 2017 the veteran whisky maker Billy Walker bought it with his partners Trisha Savage and Graham Stevenson and set out to give it a single malt identity built on heavy use of sherry casks. The 12-year-old, matured in Pedro Ximénez and oloroso sherry casks alongside virgin oak, became the core of the range.
deanston12-sb: Deanston has made whisky since 1966, when a cotton mill on the River Teith near Doune was converted into a distillery after nearly two centuries of spinning. The mill had been designed in the 1780s by Richard Arkwright, and its vaulted weaving shed now serves as a warehouse. The river still powers the site, and Deanston produces all its own electricity from hydro turbines. It also appeared in Ken Loach's 2012 film The Angels' Share.
edradour10-sb: Edradour was founded in 1825 in the hills above Pitlochry in Perthshire, and for much of its life it was celebrated as one of the smallest distilleries in Scotland, worked by a handful of people with tiny stills. In 2002 the independent bottler Andrew Symington of Signatory Vintage bought it from Pernod Ricard, and he later built a second, matching distillery on the site. Its whitewashed buildings remain one of the few that still look like the farm distilleries of the nineteenth century.
glengoyne12-sb: Glengoyne was licensed in 1833 as the Burnfoot distillery by George Connell, at the foot of Dumgoyne hill north of Glasgow, and took its current name, which the house translates as glen of the wild geese, early in the twentieth century. It sits on the Highland Line: the stills are in the Highlands, while the warehouses across the road are in the Lowlands. The distillery dries its barley with warm air rather than peat smoke and is known for its slow distillation. Ian Macleod Distillers has owned it since 2003.
tomatin12-sb: Tomatin was founded in 1897 in the hills south of Inverness, at a spot on the old drovers' road where cattle drovers are said to have filled their flasks from an illicit still. It grew dramatically in the twentieth century, and by the 1970s it had more stills than any other malt distillery in Scotland. In 1986 it became the first Scottish distillery owned by a Japanese company, led by Takara Shuzo. The name is usually translated as hill of the juniper bush.
balblair12-sb: John Ross founded Balblair in 1790 at Edderton, near the Dornoch Firth in Ross-shire, making it one of the oldest working distilleries in Scotland. In the 1890s it was rebuilt a short distance away to be close to the new railway. For more than a decade its whisky was released only as dated vintages, until in 2019 Inver House moved to age statements, with the 12-year-old as the entry point. The distillery also appears in Ken Loach's film The Angels' Share.
bennevis10-sb: Ben Nevis was founded in 1825 by John Macdonald, a tall man known as Long John, at Fort William at the foot of Britain's highest mountain, and his nickname later became the name of a well-known blend. The Macdonald family ran the distillery for generations. In 1989 the Japanese firm Nikka bought it, and since then its robust spirit has gone into Nikka's blends as well as its own single malts, of which the 10-year-old is the main release.
royallochnagar12-sb: John Begg built the New Lochnagar distillery on Deeside in 1845, near the mountain of Lochnagar and just across the river from Balmoral. When Queen Victoria and Prince Albert took up residence at Balmoral in 1848, Begg invited them to visit; they came the very next day, and the distillery soon received a royal warrant and added Royal to its name. It remains one of Diageo's smallest distilleries, and much of its whisky has gone into blends.
auchentoshan12-sb: Auchentoshan, on the north-western edge of Glasgow near the Erskine Bridge, officially dates its founding to 1823, and its name is usually translated from Gaelic as corner of the field. It is the only Scotch distillery that triple-distils all of its spirit, a technique more associated with Ireland, which gives it a light, delicate character typical of the Lowlands. The distillery was badly damaged by bombing during the Clydebank Blitz of 1941, and Suntory has owned it since the 1990s.
auchentoshanthreewood-sb: Auchentoshan has been distilling on the edge of Glasgow since about 1823 and is the only Scotch distillery to triple-distil all of its spirit. Three Wood takes that light Lowland malt through three types of cask in turn: American bourbon barrels, then Spanish oloroso sherry butts, and finally Pedro Ximénez sherry casks, which give it a much darker, sweeter profile than the house's other bottlings. The distillery was rebuilt after damage in the Clydebank Blitz and has belonged to Suntory since the 1990s.
glenkinchie12-sb: Brothers John and George Rate founded Glenkinchie in 1825 near Pencaitland in East Lothian, a farming district where barley grew around the distillery, and it took its name from the glen of the Kinchie burn, usually traced to the de Quincy family who once held the land. It has one of the largest wash stills in Scotland. The 12-year-old represents the Lowlands in Diageo's range, and the distillery is the Lowland stop on Johnnie Walker's visitor trail.
bladnochvinaya-sb: Bladnoch was founded in 1817 by brothers Thomas and John McClelland beside the River Bladnoch near Wigtown, and it is the southernmost distillery in Scotland. It closed and reopened many times, and in 1994 Raymond Armstrong, from Northern Ireland, who had first thought of turning it into holiday homes, fell for it and revived it. In 2015 the Australian entrepreneur David Prior bought it, and Vinaya, a Sanskrit word, joined the core range under his ownership.
ailsabay-sb: Ailsa Bay was built in 2007 by William Grant and Sons inside its Girvan grain distillery complex on the Ayrshire coast, and is named for the bay facing Ailsa Craig, the granite island offshore. Built to supply malt for the family's blends, it makes several styles of spirit. Its own single malt arrived in 2016, a peated whisky that the distillery first matured in small casks, to speed the spirit's contact with the wood, before moving it into larger ones, a process it calls micro-maturation.
springbank10-sb: Springbank was licensed in 1828 in Campbeltown, a town that once had around thirty distilleries and called itself the whisky capital of the world. The Mitchell family took it over in the 1830s, and their descendants still own it through J and A Mitchell. It is one of the very few distilleries in Scotland to carry out every step on site, from malting all its barley on traditional floors to bottling, and it distils its namesake spirit two and a half times. The 10-year-old is its youngest regular bottling.
springbank15-sb: Springbank dates from 1828, one of the many distilleries that once filled Campbeltown, and has been owned by the Mitchell family and their descendants since the 1830s. When the town's whisky trade collapsed between the wars, Springbank was one of the few survivors. It still malts its own barley on the floor and bottles on site, keeps old-fashioned methods such as a direct-fired wash still, and its 15-year-old is matured largely in sherry casks.
longrowpeated-sb: Longrow was first distilled in 1973 at Springbank in Campbeltown as a heavily peated, double-distilled spirit, an experiment to show that a mainland distillery could make a smoky malt to rival Islay's. The name was borrowed from an old Campbeltown distillery that had stood next door and closed in the 1890s. Springbank itself, licensed in the 1820s, makes all three of its spirits from barley malted on its own floors, and Longrow Peated, without an age statement, is now the core bottling of what grew from that experiment.
hazelburn10-sb: Hazelburn was first distilled at Springbank in 1997 as an unpeated, triple-distilled spirit, the third of the Campbeltown distillery's styles alongside Springbank and Longrow. The name comes from the old Hazelburn distillery, once one of the largest in Campbeltown, which closed in the 1920s; it is remembered as the place where Masataka Taketsuru, the Japanese distiller who later founded Nikka, served an apprenticeship in 1920.
glenscotiadoublecask-sb: Glen Scotia was founded in 1832 in Campbeltown and is one of only three working distilleries in a town that once had around thirty. It survived the collapse of the Campbeltown trade between the wars, though it fell silent several times in later decades and changed hands often. Now owned by the Loch Lomond Group, it is a compact, traditional distillery, and Double Cask is matured in bourbon barrels and finished in Pedro Ximénez sherry casks.
kilkerran12-sb: Kilkerran is the whisky of Glengyle, a Campbeltown distillery that Hedley Wright, Springbank's chairman and a descendant of the Mitchell family, revived in 2004 on the site of an older Glengyle built by William Mitchell in the 1870s and closed in the 1920s. Because the Glengyle name was already used by another company, the whisky was named Kilkerran, after the old Gaelic name for the settlement that became Campbeltown. The 12-year-old, released in 2016, was its first regular age statement.
johnniewalkerblacklabel-sb: Black Label took its name in 1909, when John Walker and Sons renamed its range of blends after the colours of their labels and adopted the Striding Man, drawn by the cartoonist Tom Browne. The firm had grown from the grocery John Walker opened in Kilmarnock in 1820, and his son Alexander had given it the square bottle and the slanting label. The 12-year-old blend became the prestige bottling that carried the name around the world.
johnniewalkerbluelabel-sb: Blue Label first appeared in 1992, under the name Johnnie Walker Oldest, as a luxury blend from a house that began with John Walker's grocery in Kilmarnock in 1820, before taking the Blue Label name. Rather than carry an age statement, it is made from a small selection of rare casks, and the company says only a tiny fraction of its stocks are good enough for it. Each bottle is individually numbered, and the blend became the flagship of the range.
johnniewalkerredlabel-sb: Red Label got its name in 1909, when John Walker and Sons renamed its range of blends after the colours of their labels, at the same time introducing the Striding Man drawn by Tom Browne. The firm had grown from John Walker's grocery in Kilmarnock, and his son Alexander had built it into an exporter, helped by a square bottle that packed neatly into crates. Red Label became the house's everyday blend and a mainstay of bars around the world.
johnniewalkergreenlabel-sb: Green Label was introduced in 1997 as Johnnie Walker Pure Malt 15 Year Old and took its current name in 2004. Unlike the house's other labels, it contains no grain whisky: it is a blended malt of single malts aged at least fifteen years, built around Talisker, Linkwood, Cragganmore and Caol Ila. Diageo withdrew it from most markets in 2012, then brought it back in 2016. Johnnie Walker itself traces back to John Walker's Kilmarnock grocery.
johnniewalkergoldlabelreserve-sb: Johnnie Walker launched Gold Label in 1995, basing it, the company says, on notes made by Sir Alexander Walker for a blend celebrating the firm's centenary, and Gold Label Reserve followed in 2013 without an age statement. It is built around Clynelish, the waxy Highland malt prized by the firm's blenders. The house itself goes back to the grocery John Walker opened in Kilmarnock, where he first sold whisky to his customers.
chivasregal12-sb: Chivas Regal began in 1909 as a 25-year-old luxury blend made by Chivas Brothers, an Aberdeen grocery and wine merchant that had received a royal warrant from Queen Victoria. Its master blender Charles Stewart Howard created it largely for the American market. After Prohibition the firm launched the 12-year-old in the United States in 1939, and it became the house's signature. Strathisla distillery in Keith, bought by the company's then owner Seagram in 1950, is its spiritual home.
chivasregal18-sb: Chivas Regal was created in 1909 by Chivas Brothers, the Aberdeen merchants who held a royal warrant from Queen Victoria, as a luxury blend for export. The 18-year-old was added in 1997 by master blender Colin Scott, who built it around rich, long-aged Speyside malts, Strathisla among them. It became the most widely known of the older Chivas blends, and the house has been owned by Pernod Ricard since 2001.
ballantinesfinest-sb: George Ballantine opened a grocery in Edinburgh in 1827, selling whiskies to his customers, and in 1865 he opened a larger wine and spirits business in Glasgow, leaving his eldest son Archibald to run the Edinburgh shop. The firm received a royal warrant from Queen Victoria in 1895. Hiram Walker bought the company in 1937 and built a huge grain distillery at Dumbarton to supply it, where a flock of geese, the Scotch Watch, guarded the warehouses for decades. Finest is the house's everyday blend.
ballantines17-sb: Ballantine's traces back to George Ballantine's grocery in Edinburgh, opened in 1827. After Hiram Walker bought the firm in 1937 it was granted a coat of arms that still appears on the bottle, and the company built its reputation abroad on aged blends. The 17-year-old, the most prominent of these, draws on malts including Miltonduff, Glenburgie, Scapa and Glentauchers.
dewarswhitelabel-sb: John Dewar opened a wine and spirits shop in Perth in 1846 and began blending whisky to sell under his own name. His sons John Alexander and Tommy turned it into an international brand, Tommy setting out on a two-year world sales tour in 1892. White Label was created in 1899 by the firm's first master blender, A. J. Cameron, and Dewar's built the Aberfeldy distillery around the same time to supply it. Bacardi has owned the brand since 1998.
dewars12-sb: Dewar's began in 1846 with John Dewar's wine and spirits shop in Perth. Its blenders have long practised a second maturation, marrying the blended malts and grains together in casks for a period before bottling, a step the house calls double ageing. The 12-year-old, once sold as Special Reserve, is built around malt from Aberfeldy, the distillery Dewar's opened in Highland Perthshire in the 1890s, where the brand's visitor centre now tells the family's story.
famousgrouse-sb: The Famous Grouse began in 1896 as The Grouse Brand, a blend created by Matthew Gloag, whose family ran a grocery and wine business in Perth. His daughter Philippa drew the grouse for the first label, and in 1905 the blend was renamed The Famous Grouse as its reputation grew. The family sold the business to Highland Distillers in 1970, and the blend has long been one of the most familiar whiskies in Scotland, its red grouse a fixture behind Scottish bars.
grantstriplewood-sb: William Grant and Sons began blending in 1898, eleven years after William Grant opened Glenfiddich, when the collapse of the Leith blenders Pattisons left the family without its main customer for malt. Grant's son-in-law Charles Gordon travelled the world selling the new blend. In the 1950s the designer Hans Schleger gave Grant's its triangular bottle. Triple Wood is matured in three types of oak cask: virgin oak, American oak and refill bourbon barrels.
cuttysark-sb: Cutty Sark was created on 23 March 1923 at a lunch held by the London wine merchants Berry Bros and Rudd, who named it after the famous tea clipper, whose own name comes from the witch's short shirt in Robert Burns's poem Tam o' Shanter. The Scottish artist James McBey designed the label. Light in colour and flavour, it found a ready market in the United States, where the story goes it was smuggled during Prohibition by the rum-runner Bill McCoy. La Martiniquaise owns it today.
jbrare-sb: Justerini and Brooks began in 1749, when Giacomo Justerini, a distiller's son from Bologna, set up a wine and spirits business in London with the English investor George Johnson. In 1831 Alfred Brooks bought out the Johnson family and the firm took its present name. J&B Rare was blended in the 1930s with American drinkers in mind as Prohibition ended, a light, pale whisky that became a fixture of bars in the United States and later in Spain. Diageo owns it today.
teachershighlandcream-sb: William Teacher began selling whisky in Glasgow in 1830, and the family built up a chain of licensed dram shops across the city. The firm registered Teacher's Highland Cream as a brand in 1884, a blend with an unusually high proportion of malt, and in 1898 opened the Ardmore distillery in Aberdeenshire to secure its peaty heart. Bottles still carry the 1830 founding date, and Ardmore's smoky Highland malt still anchors the blend.
whitehorse-sb: White Horse was brought out in the 1890s by the Mackie family firm, first under James Logan Mackie and then his nephew Peter Mackie, a forceful character who also helped build Craigellachie distillery. It was named after the White Horse Cellar, an old coaching inn on the Canongate in Edinburgh from which the stagecoach to London departed. Lagavulin, which the family owned, has always been central to the blend's smoky character.
whytemackay-sb: James Whyte and Charles Mackay went into partnership in Glasgow in 1882 as whisky merchants and blenders, and their names have stood on the blend ever since. The house is known for its extended marrying: malts are first married together in sherry butts, then blended with grain whiskies and married again before bottling, a process now sold as triple maturation. The red lion rampant of the royal arms of Scotland has long been its emblem, and its master blender Richard Paterson became one of the industry's most recognisable figures.
bellsoriginal-sb: Arthur Bell joined a Perth wine and spirits business as a salesman and by 1851 was a partner, blending malts so that his customers could rely on a consistent whisky. He was so modest about it that the Bell name did not appear on the labels until 1904, after his sons had joined the firm. In 1933 the company bought the Blair Athol and Dufftown distilleries, and Bell's became a fixture of British pubs. It has belonged to Diageo, through Guinness, since 1985.
monkeyshoulder-sb: William Grant and Sons launched Monkey Shoulder in 2005 as a blended malt, originally made from three of its Speyside single malts, Glenfiddich, Balvenie and Kininvie. Its name honours the maltmen who turned barley by hand on malting floors with wooden shovels, a repetitive job that could leave one arm hanging, a strain known as monkey shoulder; the three metal monkeys on the bottle stood for the original three malts. It was aimed squarely at bartenders and cocktails.
compassboxpeatmonster-sb: John Glaser, an American who had worked in marketing for Johnnie Walker, founded Compass Box in London in 2000 to blend Scotch from whiskies bought from distilleries across Scotland. The Peat Monster, one of its early blended malts, marries smoky Islay malts with gentler peated whisky from the mainland. Compass Box later campaigned for the right to tell drinkers exactly which whiskies, and of what ages, went into its blends, something Scotch rules restrict.
compassboxspicetree-sb: The Spice Tree was released in 2005 by Compass Box, the London whisky blender John Glaser had founded five years earlier, giving its blended malt a second maturation in casks fitted with new French oak inner staves. The Scotch Whisky Association objected that the staves were not permitted under the rules, and production stopped. Glaser reworked the method, using casks with heavily toasted French oak heads instead, and The Spice Tree returned in a form that met the regulations.
sheepdip-sb: Sheep Dip is a blended malt Scotch, made only from single malts, and its name is usually explained by an old Scottish farm joke about recording whisky in the accounts as sheep dip.
haigclub-sb: Diageo launched Haig Club in 2014 with David Beckham and the entertainment entrepreneur Simon Fuller, as a single grain Scotch made at Cameronbridge in Fife and sold in a distinctive blue bottle. The name revives that of the Haig family, among the oldest names in Scotch, who were distilling in the seventeenth century and whose John Haig founded Cameronbridge in 1824. Haig Club was pitched at drinkers new to whisky, often served with mixers.
cameronbrig-sb: John Haig founded Cameronbridge in 1824 at Windygates in Fife, and it soon became one of the first distilleries to make grain whisky in a column still, using a design by his relative Robert Stein before the Coffey still took over. Haig's firm was one of the founders of the Distillers Company in 1877. Cameron Brig, the distillery's own single grain, is one of the few grain whiskies sold under its own name. The site is now Scotland's largest grain distillery and also makes the base spirit for well-known gins and vodkas.
girvanpatentstill-sb: William Grant and Sons built the Girvan grain distillery on the Ayrshire coast in 1963, under Charles Grant Gordon, after a dispute with the Distillers Company threatened the family's supply of grain whisky for its blends; it is said to have been producing spirit within nine months of breaking ground. The Patent Still range, launched in the 2010s, takes its name from the continuous column still patented by Aeneas Coffey in 1830, the design on which Girvan's stills are based.
jameson-sb: John Jameson, a Scot from Alloa, came to Dublin and took over the Bow Street distillery, which the brand dates to 1780. Under him and his descendants it became one of the largest distilleries in the world in the nineteenth century, famous for its single pot still whiskey. After Irish Distillers was formed in 1966, production moved in the 1970s to the new Midleton distillery in County Cork. The family motto, Sine Metu, meaning without fear, still appears on the label.
jamesonblackbarrel-sb: Jameson dates from 1780, when John Jameson, a Scot from Alloa, took over the Bow Street distillery in Dublin. Black Barrel, formerly sold as Select Reserve, takes its name from the double-charred bourbon barrels in which part of it is matured, a deeper char than usual that draws out more of the wood's sweetness. It blends pot still whiskey with a higher share of small-batch grain whiskey, and is made today at the Midleton distillery in County Cork.
jameson18-sb: John Jameson took over the Bow Street distillery in Dublin in 1780, and the family name became one of the most famous in Irish whiskey. The 18-year-old, long sold as Limited Reserve, is a blend of pot still and grain whiskeys aged at least eighteen years in American bourbon barrels and Spanish oloroso sherry casks. Like all Jameson, it is now made at Midleton in County Cork, where the brand's blenders select the casks for each batch.
bushmillsoriginal-sb: Bushmills prints 1608 on its labels, the year King James I granted Sir Thomas Phillips a licence to distil in the district around the River Bush in County Antrim, though the Old Bushmills Distillery Company itself was registered in 1784. The distillery near the Giant's Causeway is one of the oldest licensed distilleries in the world and makes triple-distilled malt whiskey. Original, sometimes called White Bush, blends that malt with grain whiskey and is the house's everyday bottling.
bushmills10singlemalt-sb: Bushmills traces its licence to 1608, when Sir Thomas Phillips was granted the right to distil in the Route district of County Antrim, and the distillery company was formally established in 1784. Unlike most Irish distilleries, which built their reputations on pot still whiskey from mixed grains, Bushmills has long made spirit only from malted barley, triple-distilled. The 10-year-old single malt is matured mainly in bourbon barrels with some sherry casks. José Cuervo has owned the distillery since 2015.
bushmills16-sb: Bushmills, near the Giant's Causeway, dates its licence to 1608, and the distillery company was formally established in 1784; it survived the long twentieth-century decline of Irish whiskey that closed most of its rivals. The 16-year-old is matured separately in bourbon barrels and oloroso sherry butts, then married and finished in port pipes, a combination the distillery calls three woods. Like all Bushmills malt, it is triple-distilled from malted barley.
bushmills21-sb: Bushmills dates its licence to 1608, the year King James I allowed Sir Thomas Phillips to distil in County Antrim, and its company was formally registered in 1784. The 21-year-old is one of its rarest regular bottlings: single malt aged in bourbon barrels and oloroso sherry butts for nineteen years, then married and finished for two more in casks that held Madeira, the fortified wine of the Portuguese Atlantic island. It is released in limited quantities each year.
redbreast12-sb: Redbreast began in 1912, when the London wine and spirits firm W and A Gilbey bottled pot still whiskey from Jameson's Bow Street distillery under the name Redbreast J.J. Liqueur Whiskey. The name is said to have come from Gilbey's chairman, a keen birdwatcher, after the robin. Gilbey's stopped making it in 1985, and Irish Distillers relaunched it in 1991 as a 12-year-old, keeping alive the single pot still style made from malted and unmalted barley.
redbreast15-sb: Redbreast was first bottled in 1912 by W and A Gilbey from Jameson pot still whiskey and named after the robin by the firm's birdwatching chairman. After it disappeared in the 1980s, Irish Distillers revived it at Midleton in 1991, and the older 15-year-old followed in the 2000s. Like the rest of the range, it is single pot still whiskey, distilled from a mash of malted and unmalted barley in copper pot stills and matured in bourbon and oloroso sherry casks.
redbreast21-sb: Redbreast dates from 1912, when W and A Gilbey began bottling Jameson pot still whiskey under the robin's name. Irish Distillers brought it back in 1991 after it had vanished in the 1980s, and in 2013 released the 21-year-old, then the oldest permanent expression in the range, matured in bourbon and sherry casks. Single pot still, made from a mash of malted and unmalted barley, is a style particular to Ireland, and Redbreast became its best-known champion.
greenspot-sb: Green Spot goes back to Mitchell and Son, a Dublin firm that began as a confectioner on Grafton Street and moved into wine and spirits in 1887, maturing whiskey from Jameson's Bow Street distillery in its own casks. The firm marked its casks with spots of coloured paint to show their age, and the green-marked whiskey was the one that lasted. Through decades when Irish pot still whiskey was almost forgotten, Green Spot survived as a rare, largely local bottling, and it is now made at Midleton.
yellowspot-sb: Mitchell and Son, the Dublin firm that moved into wine and spirits in 1887, matured Jameson whiskey in its own casks and marked each cask's age with a spot of coloured paint. Yellow Spot was its 12-year-old, aged in casks that had held Malaga wine as well as bourbon barrels and sherry butts, and it was last bottled in the mid-twentieth century. In 2012 the Mitchell family and Irish Distillers relaunched it alongside the surviving Green Spot.
redspot-sb: Mitchell and Son, the Dublin firm that moved into wine and spirits in 1887, bonded whiskey from Jameson's Bow Street distillery and used spots of coloured paint to mark the ages of its casks. Red Spot was the 15-year-old, and it had been out of production for around fifty years when Irish Distillers and the Mitchell family brought it back in 2018. The new version matures for at least fifteen years in bourbon barrels, sherry butts and Marsala wine casks.
powersjohnslane-sb: James Power, a Dublin innkeeper, began distilling on Thomas Street in 1791, and by the 1820s his firm, John Power and Son, had moved to John's Lane nearby, where it grew into one of the largest distilleries in Ireland, covering six acres. The distillery closed in the 1970s when production moved to Midleton, and its buildings now house the National College of Art and Design. John's Lane, a single pot still released in 2011, recreates the heavy pot still style the old distillery was known for.
powersgoldlabel-sb: Powers goes back to 1791, when James Power began distilling in Dublin. In 1886 the family firm became one of the first Irish distillers to bottle its own whiskey rather than sell it in cask to merchants, and the gold label on those bottles gave the blend its name. Powers was for generations a fixture of Irish pubs, and since the mid-1970s it has been made at the Midleton distillery in County Cork, with a high proportion of pot still whiskey at its heart.
